title: 2d Van Der Waals Magnets: From Fundamental Physics To Applications
authors: Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, And Nuh Gedik
abstract:
Author(s): Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, and Nuh Gedik

Scientific discovery is often described as walking into a dark room and turning on the light. The discovery of 2D magnetism in van der Waals materials in 2016 was one such leap forward, removing one spatial dimension from macroscopic materials. The study of 2D magnets has challenged established theories and uncovered new phenomena. This review summarizes the current state of knowledge of magnetic phenomena in 2D van der Waals materials. The field encompasses not just the traditional study of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets but also topology, quantum and nonequilibrium dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons and spintronics, and the interaction of magnetism with light, phonons, and electric fields (multiferroics). The field is actively evolving, expanding theoretical understanding, materials capabilities, and experimental phenomenology while opening new directions for application.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025003] Published Wed May 27, 2026.
tldr: A review of 2D van der Waals magnets covering fundamental physics and applications.
motivation: To summarize the current state of knowledge and recent discoveries in 2D magnetism.
method: Review of experimental and theoretical results on 2D van der Waals magnetic materials.
result: The field encompasses ferromagnets, antiferromagnets, topology, quantum dynamics, and spintronics.
conclusion: 2D van der Waals magnets are an actively evolving field with expanding theoretical and experimental understanding.

title: Kagome Metals
authors: Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, And Stephen D. Wilson
abstract:
Author(s): Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, and Stephen D. Wilson

The kagome lattice is a two-dimensional tiling of hexagons and triangles named after a Japanese basket weaving technique. Its geometry gives rise to highly frustrated interactions and interference effects experienced by electrons and their multiple degrees of freedom. In metals, the exploration of materials with kagome conduction networks is driven by predictions of realizing new electronic states where these interference effects are dominant, amplifying electronic interactions and many-body effects. In these kagome metals, these amplified correlation effects in combination with spin-orbit coupling and other forms of frustration have given rise to a wealth of phenomena beyond expectations. These include unusual states and responses born from topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, sublattice interference effects at saddle points such as unconventional superconductivity, orbital antiferromagnetism and flux phases, amplified anomalous Hall effects, and electronic nematic states. This review examines the theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, with the aim of elucidating fundamental mechanisms underlying the observed exotic phenomena.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015002] Published Thu Feb 12, 2026.
tldr: A review of kagome metals, focusing on electronic states and many-body phenomena arising from the kagome lattice geometry.
motivation: To understand the exotic electronic states and responses in kagome metals, driven by frustration and interference effects.
method: Review of theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, analyzing topological flat bands, Dirac fermions, and correlation effects.
result: Identifies unconventional superconductivity, orbital antiferromagnetism, and other emergent phenomena in kagome metals.
conclusion: Kagome metals host a rich variety of quantum states due to geometric frustration and electronic correlations.

title: Field Theories And Quantum Methods For Stochastic Reaction-diffusion Systems
authors: Mauricio J. Del Razo, Tommaso Lamma, And Wout Merbis
abstract:
Author(s): Mauricio J. del Razo, Tommaso Lamma, and Wout Merbis

The exchange of energy and molecules in a living cell, the spread of opinions through a society, and the flow of traffic in a crowded city are very different phenomena, yet they are all examples of complex systems composed of many agents that interact with each other and exchange energy or particles with the environment. These systems can be modeled as stochastic reaction-diffusion systems. In this pedagogical review, the authors apply powerful field-theoretic methods to these systems, unifying diverse approaches under a single framework. The methods are useful for handling chemical systems but also have applications in a wide range of areas such as ecology and epidemiology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015001] Published Thu Jan 22, 2026.
tldr: A pedagogical review applying field-theoretic methods to stochastic reaction-diffusion systems in chemistry, ecology, and epidemiology.
motivation: To unify diverse approaches for modeling complex systems with many interacting agents under a single field-theoretic framework.
method: The authors review and apply field-theoretic methods, such as Doi-Peliti formalism and path integrals, to stochastic reaction-diffusion systems.
result: The review demonstrates how field theories can systematically handle fluctuations and correlations in reaction-diffusion processes.
conclusion: Field-theoretic methods provide a powerful and unified tool for analyzing stochastic reaction-diffusion systems across various disciplines.

title: Spin-glass Dynamics: Experiment, Theory, And Simulation
authors: E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, And D. Yllanes
abstract:
Author(s): E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, and D. Yllanes

This review updates the field of spin glasses with broad application to a large variety of physical systems. In particular, this review tracks the progress of experiment, theory, and large-scale simulations. It highlights the importance of their synergy, from the inception of the field to the present day, and includes future opportunities for research.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045005] Published Mon Dec 15, 2025.
tldr: A review of spin-glass dynamics covering experiment, theory, and simulation.
motivation: To provide an updated overview of spin-glass research and highlight the synergy between experimental, theoretical, and computational approaches.
method: Review of experimental results, theoretical models, and large-scale simulations of spin glasses.
result: Summarizes key advances in understanding spin-glass dynamics and identifies future research opportunities.
conclusion: Spin-glass dynamics remain a rich field with broad applications, and continued interdisciplinary collaboration is essential.

title: Kitaev Quantum Spin Liquids
authors: Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, And Hae-Young Kee
abstract:
Author(s): Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, and Hae-Young Kee

Frustration in spin systems can prevent ordering even at =0, creating quantum spin liquids that have been sought since Anderson’s pioneering work in 1973 and his influential 1987 paper connecting them to high-temperature superconductivity. Kitaev’s solvable spin-1/2 models on a honeycomb lattice brought renewed attention to this field, with Jackeli and Khaliullin later revealing how to engineer Kitaev interactions in real materials. This review highlights theoretical and experimental developments in Kitaev spin liquids, emphasizing leading candidate materials and their broad topological properties such as chiral edge modes. Consequently, it provides essential insights for both experimentalists and theorists working on quantum spin liquid problems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045003] Published Wed Dec 03, 2025.
tldr: A review of Kitaev quantum spin liquids, focusing on candidate materials and topological properties.
motivation: Quantum spin liquids are exotic phases of matter that have been sought since the 1970s, and Kitaev's exactly solvable model provides a concrete platform to realize them in real materials.
method: The review summarizes theoretical developments of the Kitaev model and experimental progress in candidate materials, highlighting topological properties such as chiral edge modes.
result: The paper provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of Kitaev spin liquid research, including key materials and their properties.
conclusion: Kitaev spin liquids remain an active area of research with potential connections to topological quantum computation, but the review does not present new results.

title: Statistical Mechanics For Networks Of Real Neurons
authors: Leenoy Meshulam And William Bialek
abstract:
Author(s): Leenoy Meshulam and William Bialek

Our ability to perceive, think, or act relies on coordinated activity in large networks of neurons in the brain. This review examines recent progress in connecting ideas from statistical physics, such as maximum entropy methods and the renormalization group, to quantitative experiments that record the electrical activity of thousands of neurons simultaneously. This quantitative bridge between the new data and statistical physics models uncovers new, quantitatively reproducible behaviors and makes clear that abstract theoretical principles in studies of the brain can have the level of predictive power that we expect in other areas of physics.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045002] Published Thu Nov 06, 2025.
tldr: This review applies statistical physics methods like maximum entropy and renormalization group to analyze neural network activity in the brain.
motivation: Understanding how coordinated activity in large neural networks underlies perception, thought, and action requires quantitative models bridging data and theory.
method: The authors review recent progress using maximum entropy models and renormalization group techniques to analyze recordings from thousands of neurons simultaneously.
result: These statistical physics approaches uncover reproducible behaviors and demonstrate that abstract theoretical principles can achieve predictive power comparable to other areas of physics.
conclusion: Statistical mechanics provides a powerful framework for understanding neural network dynamics, but the paper is primarily a review of neuroscience applications rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: The Ups And Downs Of Internal Conversion
authors: Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, And Salvy P. Russo
abstract:
Author(s): Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, and Salvy P. Russo

This review examines the theoretical methods used to describe the photophysical process of internal conversion in quantum systems. These models explore all facets of the nonradiative mechanism, and the review presents an outlook on how they can be incorporated in studies relevant to applications, for example, in photonics and energy harvesting.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035003] Published Tue Sep 16, 2025.
tldr: A review of theoretical methods for internal conversion in quantum systems, with applications in photonics and energy harvesting.
motivation: To understand and model the nonradiative relaxation process of internal conversion, which is important for applications like photonics and energy harvesting.
method: The paper reviews various theoretical models and methods used to describe internal conversion, including quantum dynamics and nonadiabatic coupling approaches.
result: The review summarizes the current state of theoretical understanding and identifies key challenges and opportunities for incorporating these models into applied studies.
conclusion: Internal conversion is a complex process that requires advanced theoretical methods, and further development is needed to fully exploit it in practical applications.

title: Colloquium: Quantum Properties And Functionalities Of Magnetic Skyrmions
authors: Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, And Christos Panagopoulos
abstract:
Author(s): Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, and Christos Panagopoulos

Skyrmions are topological field configurations that were first discussed in the context of high-energy theory. In recent years, skyrmionic spin patterns in solid-state systems have received much attention, in part for their promising application potential. This Colloquium discusses quantum-mechanical aspects of such magnetic skyrmions, both for the interactions that underlie skyrmion formation and for quantum features of the skyrmions themselves.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 031001] Published Tue Jul 08, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews quantum properties and functionalities of magnetic skyrmions, focusing on their topological nature and potential applications.
motivation: Magnetic skyrmions are promising for spintronic devices, but their quantum aspects are less explored. This review aims to bridge the gap between classical skyrmion physics and quantum mechanics.
method: The paper surveys theoretical and experimental work on skyrmion formation, quantum interactions, and quantum features of skyrmions, including quantum tunneling and entanglement.
result: It highlights that skyrmions can exhibit quantum behavior such as quantum depinning and may serve as qubits, but many quantum properties remain to be experimentally verified.
conclusion: Skyrmions offer a rich platform for studying topological quantum phenomena, but their integration into quantum information processing requires further research.

title: Spin-dependent Exotic Interactions
authors: Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, And Dmitry Budker
abstract:
Author(s): Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, and Dmitry Budker

This review presents a comprehensive summary of theoretical investigations and experimental searches for spin-dependent interactions beyond the standard model. These interactions may be mediated by various types of exotic bosons, and their existence and properties may, in turn, explain the nature of dark matter and dark energy. The described experiments also probe the discrete fundamental symmetries of nature.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025005] Published Tue Jun 24, 2025.
tldr: A comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental searches for spin-dependent exotic interactions beyond the standard model, including their possible mediation by exotic bosons and implications for dark matter and dark energy.
motivation: To understand the nature of dark matter and dark energy, and to probe fundamental symmetries of nature through spin-dependent interactions beyond the standard model.
method: The paper reviews theoretical frameworks for spin-dependent exotic interactions and summarizes experimental searches using various techniques such as atomic magnetometry, torsion balances, and precision spectroscopy.
result: The review catalogs current constraints on coupling constants and interaction ranges for various exotic boson mediators, and identifies promising avenues for future experiments.
conclusion: Spin-dependent exotic interactions remain a viable window into new physics, and ongoing experimental improvements will continue to tighten constraints or potentially discover new forces.

title: Colloquium: Materials That Exceed Classical Thermodynamic Bounds On Properties
authors: Roderic S. Lakes
abstract:
Author(s): Roderic S. Lakes

Classical thermodynamic bounds provide constraints on values that are expected in measurements of certain physical properties. In a variety of fields, some measurements exceed these bounds. This apparent violation of thermodynamics arises because the measurements are made in ways that violate the underlying assumptions made when deriving these bounds. This Colloquium describes a wide variety of circumstances where such violations occur and which of the underlying assumptions are violated in each case. It also describes how interesting material properties can be developed using materials designed to violate these assumptions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021002] Published Wed May 14, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews materials that appear to exceed classical thermodynamic bounds on properties, explaining the violations by examining underlying assumptions.
motivation: Classical thermodynamic bounds are often assumed to be fundamental limits, but some measurements exceed them; understanding why can lead to novel materials.
method: The paper surveys a wide variety of circumstances where measured properties exceed classical bounds and identifies which assumptions are violated in each case.
result: It shows that apparent violations arise because measurements are made in ways that violate assumptions (e.g., equilibrium, homogeneity) used in deriving the bounds.
conclusion: Materials can be designed to deliberately violate these assumptions, enabling properties that surpass classical thermodynamic bounds.

title: Colloquium: Synthetic Quantum Matter In Nonstandard Geometries
authors: Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, And Christof Weitenberg
abstract:
Author(s): Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, and Christof Weitenberg

This Colloquium presents ways to implement fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems. The study of quantum many-body physics in these exotic geometries permits simulation of phenomena from topology in condensed matter to models of gravity and cosmology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 011001] Published Tue Mar 25, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews experimental and theoretical implementations of fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems for simulating quantum many-body physics.
motivation: To explore quantum many-body phenomena in nonstandard geometries that are difficult to realize in conventional settings, such as topology and gravity analogs.
method: The paper surveys various platforms (ultracold atoms, photonics, electronic systems) and techniques for engineering synthetic lattices with fractal, curved, or higher-dimensional geometries.
result: It provides a comprehensive overview of current capabilities and challenges in simulating exotic geometries, highlighting connections to condensed matter topology and cosmological models.
conclusion: Synthetic quantum matter in nonstandard geometries is a rapidly advancing field with potential to uncover new physics, but it remains largely exploratory and not directly aligned with the user's core research directions.

title: Self-aligning Polar Active Matter
authors: Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, And Amir Shee
abstract:
Author(s): Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, and Amir Shee

What if active units could align–or even antialign–their orientation with their own velocity? This intriguing self-alignment property unlocks a spectrum of fascinating behaviors, from single self-propelled particles orbiting in harmonic traps to transformative collective phenomena like synchronized motion in dense or solid elastic assemblies. Unlike systems where units simply mimic their neighbors, self-alignment fundamentally reshapes how motion emerges, paving the way for groundbreaking discoveries in biology, smart materials, and robotics. This review uncovers the hidden power of self-alignment in active systems, introduces a unified mathematical and conceptual framework, explores existing models of self-alignment, and highlights its transformative impact on the study and real-world applications of active systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015007] Published Thu Mar 20, 2025.
tldr: A review of self-alignment in polar active matter, covering single-particle and collective behaviors.
motivation: To unify the understanding of self-alignment in active systems and its implications for biology, smart materials, and robotics.
method: Review of existing models and experimental observations, presenting a unified mathematical and conceptual framework.
result: Identifies that self-alignment fundamentally reshapes motion, enabling phenomena like orbiting and synchronized motion.
conclusion: Self-alignment is a key property in active matter with broad applications, but the paper is a review without novel technical contributions to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Massive Quantum Systems As Interfaces Of Quantum Mechanics And Gravity
authors: Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, And Clara C. Wanjura
abstract:
Author(s): Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, and Clara C. Wanjura

The authors review theories and experimental state-of-the-art efforts to study the effects of gravity on massive quantum systems. Classical gravity is the least precisely tested natural force and may be addressed via precision quantum probes. Experiments testing whether the quantum nature of gravity causes decoherence and collapse of matter-wave functions and whether it can mediate entanglement between separate massive particles are underway, and their results will guide the theoretical description of gravity effects on a laboratory scale.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015003] Published Thu Feb 13, 2025.
tldr: A review of theoretical and experimental efforts to study gravity's effects on massive quantum systems, including tests of quantum gravity and matter-wave interferometry.
motivation: Classical gravity is the least precisely tested natural force, and massive quantum systems may serve as probes to study gravity's quantum nature.
method: The paper reviews theories of gravity-induced decoherence, collapse models, and entanglement mediation, alongside experimental platforms such as matter-wave interferometry and optomechanics.
result: Current experiments are approaching the regime where quantum effects of gravity could be observed, but no definitive evidence has been found yet.
conclusion: Massive quantum systems offer a promising avenue to test quantum gravity, and ongoing experiments will guide future theoretical developments.

title: Classical Field Simulation Of Vortex Lattice Melting In A Two-dimensional Fast Rotating Bose Gas
authors: Sálvio J Bereta, Lucas Madeira, Mônica A Caracanhas, Hélène Perrin And Romain Dubessy
abstract: We present a classical field simulation study of the thermal melting of a two-dimensional (2D) vortex lattice in a rotating Bose gas, focusing on the role of finite-size effects on the melting temperature. This work constitutes a numerical continuation of the recent experimental investigation reported in (Sharma 2024 Phys. Rev. Lett.133 143401), which addressed the thermal melting of a vortex lattice in a quasi-2D Bose gas. Using the stochastic projected Gross–Pitaevskii equation in a harmonic plus quartic trap, we simulate the finite-temperature equilibrium state and extract vortex configurations from density snapshots. Clear signatures of the two-step Kosterlitz–Thouless–Halperin–Nelson–Young melting scenario are identified. Our simulations enable a detailed characterization of the crystalline, hexatic, and liquid phases through correlation functions quantifying the translational and orientational order and through defect statistics. Finite-size effects are shown to play a crucial role at lower rotation frequencies, affecting the proliferation of lattice defects.
tldr: This paper simulates vortex lattice melting in a rotating Bose gas using classical field methods, focusing on finite-size effects.
motivation: To understand the thermal melting of vortex lattices in two-dimensional Bose gases, building on recent experiments.
method: Uses the stochastic projected Gross–Pitaevskii equation to simulate finite-temperature equilibrium states and extract vortex configurations.
result: Identifies a two-step Kosterlitz–Thouless–Halperin–Nelson–Young melting scenario and shows that finite-size effects significantly affect defect proliferation at lower rotation frequencies.
conclusion: The simulations provide detailed characterization of crystalline, hexatic, and liquid phases, highlighting the importance of finite-size effects.

title: Direct Derivation Of The Modified Langevin Noise Formalism From The Canonical Quantization Of Macroscopic Electromagnetism
authors: A Ciattoni
abstract: The modified Langevin noise formalism (MLNF) models the interaction of the quantized electromagnetic field with an arbitrary lossy magneto-dielectric object placed in vacuum using three types of non-interacting bosonic polaritons: scattering, electric, and magnetic. These respectively represent free-space photons scattered by the object, and photons radiated by quantized electric and magnetic dipolar sources embedded within its volume. Recently (Ciattoni 2024 Phys. Rev. A110 013707), this formalism was justified from the canonical quantization of macroscopic electromagnetism (CQME) (Philbin 2010 New J. Phys.12 123008) in the Heisenberg picture. This was achieved by identifying the polariton operators within the formal solution of the macroscopic Maxwell equations, assuming they obey bosonic commutation relations to retrieve the canonical ones, and showing they diagonalize the CQME Hamiltonian. However, the explicit functional dependence of these polaritons on the underlying canonical field operators remained undetermined. In this paper, we derive the exact analytical expressions for the polariton operators in terms of the canonical CQME field operators. Using these mappings, we provide a direct and rigorous derivation of the MLNF from the canonical theory in the Schrödinger picture. Our derivation is structured in three foundational steps: 1) adopting the derived analytical expressions as the constitutive definitions of the polariton operators; 2) mathematically proving that these operators are strictly bosonic as a direct consequence of the canonical commutation relations; and 3) demonstrating that they exactly diagonalize the macroscopic CQME Hamiltonian.
tldr: This paper derives explicit analytical expressions for polariton operators in the modified Langevin noise formalism from canonical quantization of macroscopic electromagnetism.
motivation: The modified Langevin noise formalism (MLNF) models quantized electromagnetic field interaction with lossy media, but the explicit functional dependence of polariton operators on canonical field operators was unknown.
method: The authors derive exact analytical mappings for scattering, electric, and magnetic polariton operators in terms of canonical field operators, prove they satisfy bosonic commutation relations, and show they diagonalize the Hamiltonian.
result: The derived polariton operators are strictly bosonic and diagonalize the macroscopic CQME Hamiltonian, providing a rigorous derivation of MLNF from canonical theory in the Schrödinger picture.
conclusion: This work establishes a direct and rigorous connection between MLNF and canonical quantization, but it is a technical result in macroscopic quantum electrodynamics without direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: A Frequency-domain Identifiability Law For Deterministic Reconstruction Of Complex Networks Under Partial Observability
authors: Tianlong Fan And Linyuan Lü Xiaoxiao Liang
abstract: Inferring network architecture from partial behavioral observations is central to computational studies of complex systems, with implications for detecting covert actors in terrorist networks, localizing unobserved brain regions, and revealing latent molecular regulators. Focusing on evolutionary game dynamics, we uncover an empirically consistent frequency-domain regularity: the aggregated magnitude of the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) of a node’s payoff time series scales linearly with its structural degree, , across tested topologies and parameter regimes. Leveraging this structure–behavior scaling, we develop a deterministic inference framework that (i) estimates degrees directly from DFT spectra via a single global-slope fit, and (ii) uses brief, identifiability-oriented local interventions (‘suppress-and-measure’) to reveal adjacencies through intervention-induced spectral drops. Discrepancies between estimated degree and revealed neighbors deterministically enumerate external edges to hidden components and yield tight lower/upper bounds on the number of unobserved nodes. We analyze the conditions under which the scaling holds, quantify deviations under structural heterogeneity, and characterize sample-length dependence. Experiments on synthetic and empirical networks demonstrate accurate topology recovery, robustness to stochasticity, and scalability to thousand-node graphs, with consistent gains over causality-, correlation-, information-, and likelihood-based baselines. These results establish a DFT-based route to structure discovery under partial observability, translating local spectral measurements into actionable structural information.
tldr: This paper uses frequency-domain analysis of payoff time series to infer network structure under partial observability, focusing on evolutionary game dynamics.
motivation: Inferring network architecture from partial behavioral observations is important for detecting covert actors, localizing brain regions, and revealing molecular regulators.
method: The authors discover a linear scaling between the DFT magnitude of node payoff time series and its degree, and develop a deterministic inference framework using spectral measurements and local interventions.
result: The method accurately recovers network topology, provides bounds on unobserved nodes, and outperforms baselines on synthetic and empirical networks.
conclusion: The DFT-based approach offers a new route to structure discovery under partial observability, translating local spectral measurements into structural information.

title: Strong Field Ionized Electron Trajectories Driven By Squeezed Light
authors: Alex Schimmoller And Alexandra S Landsman
abstract: In atomic strong field ionization, a photoelectron’s motion is largely determined by the laser pulse’s expected electric field, as well as the atomic potential. However, when the ionization is performed by squeezed light, the photon’s quantum statistics can modify these dynamics. In this work, we generalize the classical trajectory Monte–Carlo technique to study strong field ionization by squeezed states of light. We find that electrons driven by phase-squeezed pulses exhibit increases in longitudinal momentum consistent with what is expected from the field statistics. Meanwhile, the transverse momentum distribution shows varying influence of ‘hard’ and ‘soft’ rescattering off the Coulomb potential, and the proportion of electrons recaptured as Rydberg states decreases monotonically with the amount of squeezed light applied. This work demonstrates the added experimental control over ultrafast electron dynamics achievable by tuning light’s quantum statistics, as well as the essential role of the atomic potential in strong field ionization.
tldr: This paper studies electron trajectories in strong field ionization driven by squeezed light, focusing on the effect of quantum statistics on electron dynamics.
motivation: To understand how squeezed light modifies electron dynamics in strong field ionization, potentially offering new control over ultrafast processes.
method: Generalized classical trajectory Monte-Carlo technique to simulate ionization by squeezed states of light.
result: Phase-squeezed pulses increase longitudinal momentum; transverse momentum distribution shows varying rescattering effects; Rydberg recapture decreases with squeezing.
conclusion: Squeezed light provides additional experimental control over ultrafast electron dynamics, but the atomic potential remains essential.

title: Uniaxial-stress-induced Magnetic Transitions In The Triangular-lattice Antiferromagnet PdCrO2
authors: Nina Stilkerich, Tobias Ritschel, Hilary M L Noad, Richard Waite, Dmitry Khalyavin, Kousuke Ishida, Pascal Manuel, Fabio Orlandi, Seunghyun Khim, Elena Gati, Andrew P Mackenzie, Jochen Geck And Clifford W Hicks
abstract: Uniaxial stress is a promising method to tune magnetic frustration, allowing its effects to be studied in a precise way. In this work, uniaxial stress is applied to the triangular-lattice antiferromagnet PdCrO . The Cr–Cr magnetic interaction is very sensitive to interatomic separation, so laboratory-achievable stress can induce substantial changes in magnetic structure. Results from three types of measurement are presented: x-ray diffraction, the stress–strain relationship, and neutron diffraction. The combined data show that the elastic moduli of PdCrO are strongly affected by stress-induced changes in magnetic structure. A new, first-order stress-induced magnetic transition is observed, at which the lattice constant shrinks by 0.21%. The lattice stiffens dramatically across this transition: the Young’s modulus increases by GPa, and the Poisson ratio falls from to . This stiffening indicates that the magnetic order ‘locks,’ that is, becomes insensitive to lattice strain. This locking might occur because the new stress-induced magnetic order nests the Fermi surface of the Pd sheets. Other frustrated magnets, including candidate spin liquids, may show similarly strong coupling between magnetic and elastic degrees of freedom.
tldr: This paper studies stress-induced magnetic transitions in the triangular-lattice antiferromagnet PdCrO2, focusing on the coupling between magnetic order and elastic properties.
motivation: To understand how uniaxial stress can tune magnetic frustration and induce new magnetic phases in frustrated magnets.
method: Combined x-ray diffraction, stress-strain measurements, and neutron diffraction under uniaxial stress.
result: A first-order stress-induced magnetic transition is observed, accompanied by a 0.21% lattice contraction and dramatic stiffening of the lattice.
conclusion: The magnetic order becomes locked under stress, likely due to Fermi surface nesting, suggesting strong magnetoelastic coupling in frustrated magnets.

title: Defect Approach To Giant Graviton Dynamics
authors: Yunfeng Jiang And Xinan Zhou Junding Chen
abstract: We develop a framework of zero dimensional defects for analyzing light–light–heavy–heavy (LLHH) correlators in conformal field theories. We specifically apply this formalism to correlators of giant gravitons in super Yang–Mills to probe the nontrivial physics beyond planarity. By combining this framework with bootstrap techniques, we compute all four-point functions at strong coupling involving two maximal giant gravitons and two supergravitons of arbitrary dimensions. We identify a partially broken, higher-dimensional hidden symmetry—a defect extension of 10d hidden conformal symmetry–present at both strong and weak coupling, which allows these correlators to be packaged into a single generating function. Furthermore, we perform a systematic OPE analysis of the strong-coupling correlators, extracting the complete spectrum of anomalous dimensions for the defect-channel double-particle operators. Finally, we argue that the defect perspective provides the natural nonperturbative description for any LLHH correlator by showing that four-point conformal blocks reduce to defect two-point blocks in the heavy limit.
tldr: This paper develops a defect framework for computing LLHH correlators in conformal field theories, applied to giant gravitons in super Yang-Mills theory.
motivation: To understand non-planar corrections in AdS/CFT by studying correlators involving heavy operators like giant gravitons.
method: Combines zero-dimensional defect formalism with bootstrap techniques to compute four-point functions at strong coupling.
result: Identifies a hidden 10d conformal symmetry and obtains the complete spectrum of anomalous dimensions for defect-channel operators.
conclusion: The defect perspective provides a natural nonperturbative description for LLHH correlators in the heavy limit.

title: Direct Visualization Of Field-driven Valence Band Modulation In Electrostatically Reconfigured Graphene Devices
authors: Umidakhon Rayimjonova, Chin-Yi Huang, Yi-Cheng Weng, Elin Cartwright, Fredrik O L Johansson, Noemi Vannucchi, Pavel Dudin, Avila Jose, Pei Ding, David Muradas-Belinchón, Henry Nameirakpam, Zhaojun Li, Andreas Lindblad And M Venkata Kamalakar
abstract: Graphene with ultrathin metal-oxide layers has emerged as a scalable platform for integrated electronic, spintronic, and neuromorphic devices. The in-plane electric fields in such devices are typically inferred indirectly from transport measurements, which do not provide microscopic details of the interface potential profile. Here, we use photoemission microscopy to uncover the precise electrostatic landscape of a complete device comprising diverse, heterogeneous ultrathin metal-oxide-covered graphene junctions. Using in operando x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy with submicron resolution, we directly image the real potential profile across an entire graphene device, including regions covered by AlOx and TiOx nanometer-thick overlayers. Tracking the valence band edge under current bias and gate voltage enables quantitative analysis of internal field evolution via a spectroscopic screening factor, revealing an up to more than 50% suppression of the electric field in graphene covered with oxides, in agreement with transport measurements. This demonstrates local reconfiguration of electric fields in graphene for advanced two-dimensional (2D) device engineering and circuitry, while our operando circuit spectroscopy measurements provide a generic means to uncover intricate potential landscapes and carrier redistribution in 2D electronic and spintronic circuits.
tldr: This paper uses photoemission microscopy to directly visualize the electrostatic potential profile in graphene devices with oxide overlayers, revealing field suppression.
motivation: Understanding the microscopic electrostatic landscape in graphene devices is crucial for optimizing electronic and spintronic performance, but indirect transport measurements lack spatial detail.
method: In operando x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy with submicron resolution was used to image the valence band edge across a graphene device under bias and gate voltage, extracting a spectroscopic screening factor.
result: The electric field in graphene covered with AlOx and TiOx is suppressed by up to 50% compared to bare graphene, consistent with transport measurements.
conclusion: Operando circuit spectroscopy provides a generic method to map potential landscapes in 2D devices, enabling advanced engineering of electric fields in graphene circuits.

title: Optical Amplification With Large Goos-H$\ddot{a}$nchen Shift Driven By Non-Hermitian Bilayer Meta-Grating
authors: Xueyi Zhang Ma Luo
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31060v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical Goos-H[MATH]nchen shifts can be enhanced by resonant mode with high quality factor, such as quasi-bound states in the continuum in meta-grating. Coexistence of gain and loss in bilayer meta-grating with parity-time symmetry could transfer bound states in the continuum into lasing threshold modes with real resonant frequencies and non-zero far-field radiation. When the incident frequency approaches the resonant frequency of a lasing threshold mode, the reflected and transmitted beams are strongly amplified and undergo large Goos-H[MATH]nchen shifts. The amplitude of the Goos-H[MATH]nchen shifts, including the magnitude and sign, are proportional to the reciprocal of the imaginary part of the resonant frequencies. As the incident frequency scan across the resonant frequency of a lasing threshold mode, the imaginary part flip sign, so that the Goos-H[MATH]nchen shifts diverge as well as flip sign. Simulations of optical responses under incident of Gaussian beams with finite beam width exhibit the sign flipping of the Goos-H[MATH]nchen shift with large magnitude by fine tuning the incident frequency across the resonant frequency of a lasing threshold mode.
tldr: This paper studies optical amplification and large Goos-Hänchen shifts in a non-Hermitian bilayer meta-grating with parity-time symmetry.
motivation: To enhance Goos-Hänchen shifts using resonant modes with high quality factor and explore the effects of gain and loss in PT-symmetric structures.
method: The authors design a bilayer meta-grating with parity-time symmetry, analyze lasing threshold modes, and simulate optical responses of Gaussian beams.
result: The Goos-Hänchen shift diverges and flips sign when the incident frequency crosses the resonant frequency of a lasing threshold mode, with amplification.
conclusion: The proposed structure enables large, sign-flipping Goos-Hänchen shifts, which may have applications in optical sensing and switching.

title: On The Structure Of Optimal Free Dirichlet Regions In Mass Transportation Problems
authors: Lucas D. O'brien
abstract: ArXiv:2606.30826v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For a compactly supported probability measure [MATH] on the [MATH]-dimensional space [MATH], the average distance problem asks us to minimize the average distance functional over all compact, connected, [MATH] satisfying the Hausdorff [MATH]-measure constraint [MATH]. This problem was first introduced in 2002 by Buttazzo, Oudet, and Stepanov to study optimal transport problems with free regions on which the transport cost vanishes, and has undergone a considerable amount of research since. Most recently, Kobayashi, Kim, and the author studied the structure of these regions using the barycentre field, a tool for studying the average distance functional introduced previously by Kobayashi, Hayase, and Kim. In this paper, we build upon this work to prove in much greater generality a topological description of minimizers of the average distance problem conjectured by Buttazzo, Oudet, and Stepanov. In particular, we prove this conjecture in all dimensions in the case originally studied by these authors.
tldr: This paper studies the structure of optimal free Dirichlet regions in mass transportation problems, focusing on the average distance problem.
motivation: The average distance problem was introduced to study optimal transport with free regions where transport cost vanishes, and a conjecture about the topological structure of minimizers remained open.
method: The authors use the barycentre field, a tool for studying the average distance functional, to prove the conjecture in greater generality and in all dimensions.
result: They prove a topological description of minimizers of the average distance problem, confirming the conjecture by Buttazzo, Oudet, and Stepanov.
conclusion: The work provides a complete characterization of optimal free Dirichlet regions in the original setting, advancing the theory of mass transportation problems.

title: Fluid-Antenna-Aided Active User Detection With 1d-cnn Channel Reconstruction For Unsourced Random Access
authors: Haoyu Liang, Zhentian Zhang, Hao Jiang, Jian Dang, Zaichen Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31139v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we investigate the application of fluid antenna systems (FAS) for active user detection (AUD) in unsourced random access (URA). A channel reconstruction method based on a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) is proposed to effectively learn the nonlinear mapping from partial channel observations to the full channel vector. Furthermore, the reconstructed channel information is exploited to improve AUD performance via port selection. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed 1D-CNN channel reconstructor significantly outperforms traditional methods under varying pilot lengths, achieving superior normalized mean squared error (NMSE) performance. Additionally, the reconstructed channel substantially reduces the AUD error rate compared with conventional approaches relying on traditional antenna configurations.
tldr: This paper applies fluid antenna systems and 1D-CNN for active user detection in unsourced random access, focusing on wireless communication rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Improving active user detection in unsourced random access using fluid antenna systems and deep learning.
method: Proposes a 1D-CNN to reconstruct full channel vectors from partial observations and uses the reconstructed channel for port selection to enhance detection.
result: The 1D-CNN reconstructor achieves lower NMSE and reduces AUD error rate compared to traditional methods.
conclusion: Fluid antenna systems combined with CNN-based channel reconstruction can significantly improve active user detection performance.

title: Periodic Non-uniqueness Sets For Shift-invariant Spaces And Parity-Based Obstructions To The Frame Property For Gabor Systems
authors: Ilya Zlotnikov Alexander Ulanovskii
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31450v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The goal of this note is twofold. First, we provide explicit examples of periodic (though not necessarily lattice) sets that give rise to Gabor systems failing to form frames. Our constructions depend only on the parity of the window function [MATH]. Second, for a wide range of finite-dimensional function spaces [MATH] we show that [MATH] contains a function [MATH] such that a lattice of high density fails to generate a Gabor frame. In particular, we prove that the Gr\"ochenig-Lyubarskii theorem is sharp in the finite-dimensional space of polynomials with Gaussian weight. More precisely, for every [MATH] and every [MATH] satisfying [MATH], we give an explicit algorithm for finding an even or odd polynomial [MATH] of degree at most [MATH] such that [MATH] does not form a frame. The proofs are constructive, elementary, and based on linear algebra.

title: Gaussian Belief Propagation For Tracking With Unresolved Measurements
authors: Augustin A. Saucan, Florian Meyer, Peter Willett
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31716v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unresolved measurements occur in many inference problems where two or more hidden processes may, at times, jointly generate a single measurement. For instance, such phenomena are encountered in multiobject tracking owing to the limited resolution capabilities of practical sensors; or in camera-aided autonomous driving due to shadowing or occlusions. Substantial performance degradation, such as track losses, are incurred when unresolved measurements are not accounted for. In this paper, we address multiobject tracking under a generalized unresolved measurement model, where any subset of objects may generate a single unresolved measurement according to a probabilistic model. Our innovation lies both in modeling and algorithm-design directions. First, we develop a probability distribution for object partitions based on a model of pairwise coupling of objects and subsequently a probability distribution for object-to-measurement association variables. This generic model incorporates sensor resolution capabilities, sensor detection, and sensor noise characteristics for object groups. Second, a generic Loopy Belief Propagation (LBP) method as well as a specialized Gaussian-LBP (GLBP) algorithm are proposed that perform object state inference under the aforementioned model. In contrast to direct marginalization methods, which involve a computational complexity of [MATH], for [MATH] measurements and [MATH] objects, the proposed GLBP algorithm achieves a computational complexity on the order of [MATH]. Numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed GLBP, with estimation performance that closely matches that of exact marginalization for only a fraction of the computational resources.
tldr: This paper proposes a Gaussian Belief Propagation algorithm for multiobject tracking with unresolved measurements, focusing on computational efficiency.
motivation: Unresolved measurements in multiobject tracking cause performance degradation; existing methods are computationally expensive.
method: The authors develop a probabilistic model for object partitions and measurement associations, then propose a Loopy Belief Propagation method and a specialized Gaussian-LBP algorithm for inference.
result: The GLBP algorithm achieves computational complexity O(NM) compared to exponential complexity of exact methods, with estimation performance close to exact marginalization.
conclusion: The proposed GLBP algorithm effectively handles unresolved measurements in multiobject tracking with significantly reduced computational cost.

title: The Cooperation Ceiling: Extrinsic Population Dynamics And The Intrinsic Escape
authors: Harry Foster, Vince Knight, Sebastian Krapohl
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31740v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evolutionary game theory provides a framework by which to study the emergence of cooperation in a population of self-interested actors. In such a framework, players' decisions on whether or not to cooperate evolve according to decision rules called population dynamics. However, often games are studied under the assumption that all individuals play under the same conditions, and many common choices of update rule are not well suited for a heterogeneous population. In this paper, we categorise and compare four different population dynamics in such a population as ``extrinsic'', where players learn by looking outward at the payoffs of other players, and ``intrinsic'', where players look inwardly at their own attributes or potential payoffs. We show that extrinsic population dynamics admit a ceiling on the rate of cooperation which can be exceeded by intrinsic population dynamics, and demonstrate this using the public goods game with heterogeneous contributions.
tldr: This paper studies cooperation in evolutionary game theory using extrinsic and intrinsic population dynamics, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Understanding cooperation in heterogeneous populations is a classic problem in evolutionary game theory.
method: The authors categorize and compare four population dynamics (extrinsic vs intrinsic) and test them in a public goods game with heterogeneous contributions.
result: Extrinsic dynamics impose a ceiling on cooperation rates, while intrinsic dynamics can exceed that ceiling.
conclusion: Intrinsic population dynamics may better promote cooperation in heterogeneous settings.

title: The Logic Of Data Access And Data Exchanges
authors: Alexandru Baltag (ILLC, University Of Amsterdam), Sonja Smets
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31858v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate a new logic that extends Dynamic Epistemic Logic (DEL), by combining standard epistemic modalities for (individual and distributed) propositional knowledge with operators for (conditional) non-propositional knowledge of a number (in which an agent or a group have knowledge of the value of some variable x, conditional on some additional information). We also generalize these operators, by considering formulas that express the fact that an agent or group can (conditionally) narrow down the possible values of the variable x to at most N possibilities (for some natural number N). In order to name and compare such hypothetical values, we extend the logic further with definite descriptions based on minimization operators, denoting the least of the N possible values of x (according to some fixed order) that are considered possible by the agent or group. On this static base, we consider DEL-style extensions with dynamic modalities for general 'data-exchange events' (covering private and public propositional announcements, but also secret hacking of a private database, or public sharing of one's data via open-source repositories, etc.). In such scenarios, whole 'chunks' of information may be exchanged or modified: once access to a given source is gained, all the 'data' stored at that specific location becomes available. We give complete axiomatizations for the resulting logics, and prove their decidability and co-expressivity.
tldr: This paper extends Dynamic Epistemic Logic with operators for non-propositional knowledge of numbers and data-exchange events, providing complete axiomatizations and decidability results.
motivation: The authors aim to model scenarios where agents have knowledge about numerical values and can exchange entire data chunks, which is not captured by standard epistemic logic.
method: They define a logic combining epistemic modalities with operators for conditional knowledge of a number and minimization operators, and add dynamic modalities for data-exchange events. Completeness and decidability are proved via standard techniques.
result: The logic is shown to be decidable and expressively equivalent to a fragment of first-order logic, with complete axiomatizations provided.
conclusion: The work contributes to the foundations of epistemic logic but does not directly address quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Tricky Tension
authors: Warren J. Jasper

conclusion: The classification aids in interpreting experimental SANS data from vortex-state nanoparticles.

title: Are Neural Networks Collision Resistant?
authors: Marco Benedetti, Andrej Bogdanov, Enrico M. Malatesta, Marc Mézard, Gianmarco Perrupato, Alon Rosen, Nikolaj I. Schwartzbach, And Riccardo Zecchina
abstract:
Author(s): Marco Benedetti, Andrej Bogdanov, Enrico M. Malatesta, Marc Mézard, Gianmarco Perrupato, Alon Rosen, Nikolaj I. Schwartzbach, and Riccardo Zecchina

A study of the computational complexity of finding collisions in a simple one-layer neural network shows that efficient algorithms fail to find collisions, a result of direct relevance for the definition of new cryptographic protocols based on machine-learning models.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021051] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the computational complexity of finding collisions in a simple one-layer neural network, showing that efficient algorithms fail to find collisions.
motivation: To explore whether neural networks can be used as cryptographic primitives by analyzing their collision resistance.
method: The authors analyze the computational complexity of finding collisions in a one-layer neural network, likely using theoretical complexity arguments and algorithmic analysis.
result: Efficient algorithms fail to find collisions in the studied neural network model.
conclusion: The result suggests potential for defining new cryptographic protocols based on machine-learning models, but the paper is not directly related to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Probing Quantum Anomalous Hall States In Twisted Bilayer ${\mathrm{WSe}}_{2}$ Via Attractive Polaron Spectroscopy
authors: Beini Gao, Mahdi Ghafariasl, Mahmoud Jalali Mehrabad, Tsung-Sheng Huang, Lifu Zhang, Deric Session, Pranshoo Upadhyay, Rundong Ma, Ghadah Alshalan, Daniel Suarez, Supratik Sarkar, Suji Park, Houk Jang, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Ming Xie, You Zhou, And Mohammad Hafezi
abstract:
Author(s): Beini Gao, Mahdi Ghafariasl, Mahmoud Jalali Mehrabad, Tsung-Sheng Huang, Lifu Zhang, Deric Session, Pranshoo Upadhyay, Rundong Ma, Ghadah Alshalan, Daniel Suarez, Supratik Sarkar, Suji Park, Houk Jang, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Ming Xie, You Zhou, and Mohammad Hafezi

Magneto-optical spectroscopy of twisted WSe
[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021037] Published Mon May 18, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports magneto-optical spectroscopy of twisted bilayer WSe2, revealing a quantum anomalous Hall phase and electric-field control of magnetic order.
motivation: To probe and control quantum anomalous Hall states in twisted bilayer WSe2, a moiré material, using optical spectroscopy.
method: Magneto-optical spectroscopy, specifically attractive polaron spectroscopy, is used to study the electronic and magnetic properties of twisted bilayer WSe2 under varying electric and magnetic fields.
result: A spontaneous quantum anomalous Hall phase is observed, and electric-field control over transitions between ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic orders is demonstrated.
conclusion: Twisted bilayer WSe2 is a platform for studying quantum anomalous Hall states and magnetic phase transitions, with potential for future quantum devices.

title: Stealthy-Hyperuniform Wave Dynamics In Two-Dimensional Photonic Crystals
authors: Maria Barsukova, Zeyu Zhang, Brian Gould, Koorosh Sadri, Christian Rosiek, Søren Stobbe, Jonas Karcher, And Mikael C. Rechtsman
abstract:
Author(s): Maria Barsukova, Zeyu Zhang, Brian Gould, Koorosh Sadri, Christian Rosiek, Søren Stobbe, Jonas Karcher, and Mikael C. Rechtsman

While disordered stealthy hyperuniform materials are expected to be largely transparent within a particular range of wavelengths, new experiments on large-scale silicon photonic crystals reveal unexpected residual scattering driven by radiative loss.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021028] Published Thu May 07, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies wave dynamics in two-dimensional photonic crystals with stealthy hyperuniform disorder, revealing unexpected residual scattering due to radiative loss.
motivation: Stealthy hyperuniform materials are expected to be transparent in certain wavelength ranges, but experiments show unexpected scattering that needs explanation.
method: Large-scale silicon photonic crystals are fabricated and characterized experimentally, with theoretical modeling of radiative loss.
result: Residual scattering is driven by radiative loss, contradicting the expectation of transparency.
conclusion: The findings highlight the importance of radiative loss in disordered photonic materials, impacting their optical properties.

title: Radiation Forces And Torques In Optics And Acoustics
authors: Ivan Toftul, Sebastian Golat, Francisco J. Rodríguez-Fortuño, Franco Nori, Yuri Kivshar, And Konstantin Y. Bliokh
abstract:
Author(s): Ivan Toftul, Sebastian Golat, Francisco J. Rodríguez-Fortuño, Franco Nori, Yuri Kivshar, and Konstantin Y. Bliokh

This review presents a unified perspective of how local energy, momentum, and spin densities in optical and acoustic wave fields induce forces and torques on particles—a topic that has captivated researchers for centuries. Applications discussed include trapping and manipulation of atoms and nanoparticles by light, sorting of biological cells by the combination of acoustics and microfluidics, and pulling forces that draw particles against the direction of wave propagation.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025002] Published Thu Apr 30, 2026.
tldr: This review unifies the description of radiation forces and torques in optical and acoustic fields, focusing on momentum and spin densities.
motivation: Understanding how wave fields exert forces and torques on particles is fundamental for applications like optical trapping and acoustic manipulation.
method: The authors present a unified theoretical framework based on local energy, momentum, and spin densities in both optical and acoustic wave fields.
result: They show that the same physical principles govern forces and torques in optics and acoustics, enabling cross-disciplinary insights.
conclusion: The unified perspective can guide future developments in particle manipulation using light and sound.

title: Using Gravitational Waves To See The First Second Of The Universe
authors: Rishav Roshan And Graham White
abstract:
Author(s): Rishav Roshan and Graham White

Gravitational waves open a unique window on the earliest times in cosmology because the dense primordial plasma, impenetrable to light or neutrinos, is transparent to gravitational waves up to the instant of the birth of the Universe. This review discusses the possible signals from the phase transitions, topological defects, and other cosmological sources, as well as a range of strategies for detection of the stochastic gravitational waves produced by the earliest events in the history of the Universe.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015001] Published Wed Jan 08, 2025.
tldr: This review discusses gravitational wave signals from the early universe, including phase transitions and topological defects.
motivation: Gravitational waves provide a unique probe of the first second of the universe, which is opaque to electromagnetic radiation.
method: The paper reviews theoretical predictions for stochastic gravitational wave backgrounds from cosmological sources and detection strategies.
result: It summarizes possible signals from phase transitions, topological defects, and other early-universe phenomena.
conclusion: Gravitational wave astronomy can reveal physics of the early universe that is otherwise inaccessible.

title: Causality Of Ultrafast Photoionization From Argon 3 S Usin...
authors: Rezvan Tahouri And Jan Marcus Dahlström
abstract: We study real-time photoionization flux at the Amusia–Cooper minimum (ACM) in argon using ab initio simulations with the relativistic time-dependent configuration-interaction singles (RTDCIS) method in length (LG) and velocity (VG) gauges. A simple analytical model is used to interpret the results, and to construct Wigner delays and Wigner distributions for both gauges and relativistic channels of the photoelectron ( with and ). The two gauges are found to produce qualitatively different ionization dynamics, with LG having positive and VG having negative Wigner delays. The advancement of several femtoseconds, found for Wigner delays in VG, raises some concern for causality when atoms are ionized by attosecond pulses that are shorter than the absolute value of the Wigner delay. Reassuringly, numerical simulations of wave packets with RTDCIS show that the electrons behave in a causal way in both gauges. Weighted delays that take into account the temporal window of excitation (or the bandwidth of the pulses) are constructed from the Wigner distribution to reach agreement between the numerical simulations and our simple wave packet model. Furthermore, a strong effect of spin–orbit coupling of the photoelectron ( ) is reported for ultrafast photoionization dynamics, and Schrödinger kitten and cat states are identified in the Wigner distributions as a result of the ACM. Our work paves the way for a deeper understanding of ultrafast photoionization and the role of causality in systems with strong electron–electron correlation effects.
tldr: This paper studies ultrafast photoionization dynamics in argon at the Amusia-Cooper minimum using ab initio simulations, focusing on causality and Wigner delays.
motivation: To understand the role of causality in ultrafast photoionization and resolve gauge-dependent Wigner delays that appear to violate causality.
method: Relativistic time-dependent configuration-interaction singles (RTDCIS) simulations in length and velocity gauges, combined with a simple analytical model and Wigner distribution analysis.
result: Length gauge yields positive Wigner delays while velocity gauge yields negative delays of several femtoseconds, but numerical wave packet simulations confirm causal behavior in both gauges.
conclusion: Weighted delays accounting for pulse bandwidth reconcile gauge differences, and spin-orbit coupling significantly affects dynamics; Schrödinger kitten/cat states are identified in Wigner distributions.

title: Nucleation Of Adamantane Clusters In Weakly Ionised Plasmas: Dispersion Cohesion, Surface Energy, And Charging
authors: Johannes Fiedler And Justas Zalieckas
abstract: The formation of molecular clusters in low-temperature plasmas is governed by an intricate interplay of dispersion interactions, electrostatic charging, and surface energetics. While chemical growth pathways have been extensively studied, the role of non-chemical interactions in determining characteristic cluster sizes remains poorly understood. In this work, we develop a unified free-energy framework for molecular clusters embedded in weakly ionised Ar/H plasmas. The approach combines first-principles calculations of the molecular polarisability of adamantane with a dielectric description of the plasma response, including collisional damping and plasma screening. Dispersion interactions are treated as a bulk-like cohesive contribution with a physically motivated microscopic cutoff, while electrostatic charging is described within floating-potential theory. We show that, for realistic discharge parameters, the total free energy does not generally exhibit an effective equilibrium radius. Instead, the free-energy landscape is characterised by a nucleation barrier with an effective critical radius separating subcritical clusters from downhill growth. By mapping this nucleation threshold scale as a function of pressure, electron temperature, and gas composition, we demonstrate that plasma conditions provide a systematic control over the nucleation scale. Our results suggest that experimentally observed steady cluster sizes in weakly ionised plasmas are governed by kinetic balance rather than free-energy minimisation, and that gas composition and plasma parameters can be used as effective control knobs for early-stage cluster formation.
tldr: This paper studies nucleation of adamantane clusters in weakly ionised plasmas using a free-energy framework, focusing on dispersion cohesion, surface energy, and charging.
motivation: The role of non-chemical interactions in determining characteristic cluster sizes in low-temperature plasmas is poorly understood.
method: A unified free-energy framework combining first-principles polarisability calculations with a dielectric plasma response model, including collisional damping and plasma screening.
result: The free-energy landscape exhibits a nucleation barrier with an effective critical radius; no equilibrium radius exists; cluster sizes are governed by kinetic balance.
conclusion: Plasma conditions (pressure, electron temperature, gas composition) can systematically control the nucleation scale in weakly ionised plasmas.

title: Vortex Solitons In Disclination Quasicrystals
authors: Hua Zhong, Yaroslav V Kartashov, Yongdong Li, Fangwei Ye And Yiqi Zhang
abstract: Quasicrystals are ubiquitous in nature. They represent unique aperiodic materials featuring long-range order that occupy an intermediate niche between exactly periodic and disordered materials. These properties are reflected in the unusual evolutionary dynamics of excitations and unique localization properties of linear eigenmodes supported by quasicrystals. In particular, being the structures characterized by discrete rotational symmetry of order , photonic quasicrystals can support the stable propagation of linear vortex-carrying light beams and vortex solitons. However, the impact of discrete rotational symmetry of quasicrystals on the properties of vortex light states has not been investigated so far, as only the systems constructed using the simplest Penrose tiling or corresponding optically induced Penrose lattices are considered in this context. Here, we propose a broad class of quasicrystals with global topological defects—disclinations—introduced into their structure that allows to produce novel quasicrystalline structures with any desired order of discrete rotational symmetry from the basic Penrose structure. Such global topological deformation substantially enriches the linear spectrum of quasicrystals, allowing them to support new types of linear vortex states and bifurcating from them families of stable thresholdless vortex solitons with unusual intensity and phase distributions. We find two different classes of stable vortex solitons comprising in-phase or out-of-phase pairs of closely located bright spots, with total intensity distribution reflecting a particular discrete rotational symmetry of the quasicrystal with disclination. Remarkably, even low-charge vortex solitons can be stable in quasicrystals with disclinations, whereas stability intervals for them broaden with the decrease of the discrete rotational symmetry of quasicrystals. Our results extend the theory of localization in quasicrystals to structures with global topological deformation, highlighting emerging prospects for the robust transmission of power or information arising in these systems.
tldr: This paper studies vortex solitons in photonic quasicrystals with disclinations, focusing on nonlinear wave propagation and localization.
motivation: To understand how global topological defects (disclinations) in quasicrystals affect the properties of vortex light states, which have not been investigated before.
method: The authors propose a class of quasicrystals with disclinations, analyze their linear spectrum, and numerically find families of stable thresholdless vortex solitons.
result: Two classes of stable vortex solitons are found, with stability intervals broadening as discrete rotational symmetry decreases.
conclusion: The results extend localization theory to quasicrystals with topological deformations, offering potential for robust transmission of power or information.

title: Record-high Glass Coefficient In The Shift Current Response Of A Ferroelectric Halide Perovskite
authors: Koma Mikimasao Nakamuraasahi Yamadagurvan Bosserkiyohiro Adachidaisuke Hashizumenaoki Ogawasatoshi Okamotoyoshinori Tokuramasashi Kawasakiahttps://ror.org/057zh3y96department Of Applied Physics And Quantum-Phase Electronics Center, The University Of Tokyo, Tokyo 113-8656, Japanbhttps://ror.org/057zh3y96department Of Fundamental Engineering, Institute Of Industrial Science, The University Of Tokyo, Tokyo 153-8505, Japanchttps://ror.org/03gv2xk61riken Center For Emergent Matter Science, Wako 351-0198, Japandriken Baton Zone Program, Wako 351-0198, Japanehttps://ror.org/01dq60k83department Of Physics, Graduate School Of Science, Tohoku University, Sendai 980-8578, Japanfsumitomo Chemical Co., Ltd, Tokyo 103-6020, Japanghttps://ror.org/057zh3y96tokyo College, The University Of Tokyo, Tokyo 113-8656, Japan
